analysis.one_liner: Replaces the federal income and estate taxes with a simpler graduated income tax and a tax on business profits.
analysis.headline: The bill to scrap the income tax and estate tax in favor of a simplified 15-30% tax with a refundable payroll-tax credit died in committee with zero cosponsors and never got a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 134 would have wiped out the individual and corporate income taxes and replaced them with one "Simplified USA Tax" in two parts: a graduated individual tax at 15%, 25%, and 30% with a family living allowance, and a business tax of 8% to 12% on gross profits. It would have refunded the payroll taxes taken out of low-wage workers' paychecks, let anyone put unlimited savings into a tax-free Roth IRA, exempted exports while taxing imports at roughly 11%, and repealed the estate and gift taxes outright. The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers would gain the most directly: the bill makes the payroll (FICA) tax withheld from their paychecks a credit against income tax, refundable in cash if it exceeds what they owe, effectively erasing the most regressive tax they pay while leaving Social Security benefits untouched. Families would gain a generous family living allowance, larger exemptions, a deduction of up to $4,000 per student for college tuition, and a much shorter tax return. Wealthy households and heirs would gain the outright repeal of the estate and gift tax and the right to shelter unlimited savings in Roth IRAs. Corporations and other businesses would gain a much lighter business tax (8% on profits up to $150,000, 12% above) with immediate expensing of investment and tax-free export revenues.

how_it_helps.text: It turns the payroll tax into a refundable credit: every dollar of FICA withheld from a worker's paycheck is credited against income tax, and if the credit exceeds what the worker owes, the difference is paid back in cash — so a low-wage worker's Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes are effectively refunded, without touching the trust funds or benefits.

It shields basic living costs from tax through a family living allowance ($4,840 for a single filer, $8,140 for a couple, inflation-indexed) plus $2,700 personal exemptions, and allows a deduction for up to $4,000 of college tuition and fees per student ($12,000 per return).

It would have radically simplified filing: only a few deductions (home mortgage interest on acquisition debt, education, charity), and the bill's own findings promise a return 'a small fraction the size of Form 1040' that taxpayers can calculate themselves with little risk of an IRS dispute.

It ends the double taxation of saving: anyone could contribute up to their entire income to a Roth IRA and never pay tax on the earnings, and contributions could continue after age 70½ with no forced withdrawals.
It eliminates the estate and gift tax entirely, so family businesses and heirs would no longer face tax on inherited wealth at death.

analysis.who_pays: Workers with employer-provided health insurance would pay first: the bill counts the cost of employer-paid health, disability, and life coverage as taxable income, a large new tax bill for millions of middle-income employees. Consumers who buy imported goods would pay through an import tax of roughly 11% of customs value, which businesses pass along in prices. Businesses would pay the new 8-12% gross-profits tax, though far below the corporate income tax rates it replaces. Whoever absorbed any revenue gap left by the estate tax repeal and lower business rates — the bill asserts individuals and businesses would pay about the same shares as under current law, but it was never independently scored — and users of home-equity loans, whose interest deduction is eliminated.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employees with job-based health coverage, import consumers

drawbacks.text: It taxes employer-paid health insurance as employee income, converting one of the largest existing middle-class tax breaks into a new tax liability for workers with job-based coverage — a real cost the bill's own text imposes on ordinary employees.
Repealing the estate and gift tax benefits only the largest estates, which pay virtually all of that tax, making Title V a large, permanent transfer to very wealthy families.
The 11% import tax would raise prices on imported goods, functioning as a consumption tax that falls hardest on households that spend most of their income.

Unlimited Roth IRA contributions are worth the most to households with large amounts to shelter, and the business tax (8% to 12% of gross profits) is far below the corporate income tax rates it replaces, so the distributional claims of neutrality rest on the bill's own findings rather than an independent score.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The refundable payroll-tax credit is a genuinely large progressive benefit — nothing else in the tax code offsets the payroll tax for low-wage workers — and the simplification and education deduction are real gains for working families. But those gains are bought partly at other working people's expense: new tax on employer health coverage and an 11% import tax that shows up in prices. Meanwhile the estate tax repeal and the much lighter business tax send large, unconditional benefits up the income ladder, and the bill's promise that everyone pays 'about the same' share was never tested by an independent score. As drafted, the bill is a serious pro-worker idea grafted onto a tax overhaul whose biggest winners are wealthy families and businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Phil English introduced the Simplified USA Tax Act on January 6, 1999, the first day of the 106th Congress, as a full replacement for the individual and corporate income taxes.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the panel that writes tax law.

The proposal would have replaced the current code with a 15/25/30% graduated individual tax, an 8-12% tax on business gross profits with exports exempted and imports taxed, a refundable payroll-tax credit for workers, and outright repeal of the estate and gift tax.
Not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill received no cosponsors at any point in the two-year Congress.
No hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed; the last entry in the bill's history is the January 6, 1999 referral, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill dead in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No taxpayer's bill changed, so the immediate winners were the status quo and everyone who would have owed more under the new code — especially workers who would have been taxed on employer health benefits and shoppers who never saw an 11% import tax. The losers were low-wage workers who would have had their payroll taxes refunded, and very wealthy estates, which kept paying the estate tax the bill would have repealed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; no taxes changed

for.name: Rep. Phil English
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Simplified USA Tax Act on the opening day of the 106th Congress; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote; its last recorded action is the January 6, 1999 referral.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that never acted on the bill while promoting his own plan to replace the income tax with a national sales tax, leaving competing overhaul proposals without committee action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no partisan split is on record; the only identifiable support was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate and gift tax outright and allows unlimited tax-free Roth IRA contributions, both of which overwhelmingly benefit the wealthiest households; the lost revenue would otherwise fund government or tax relief spread across everyone else.

The corporate income tax is replaced by an 8% to 12% tax on gross profits with immediate expensing of investment and export revenues excluded — far lighter than the rates it replaces. Some businesses, notably importers, would bear the new 11% import tax instead.

The bill taxes imports at roughly 11% of customs value while exempting exports; importers would pay it and pass the cost to consumers in higher prices, so both the industry and ordinary shoppers lose.

Employer-paid health coverage becomes taxable income to employees, raising the effective cost of job-based insurance and potentially pushing employers and workers away from it — a new burden on covered workers with uncertain consequences for insurers.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A code with only a few deductions and a return 'a small fraction the size of Form 1040' would shrink the market for paid preparers and software, while saving ordinary filers time and money.
